name: rpiboot
desc: Raspberry Pi USB boot tool for Compute Modules
why: Uses USB to expose a Compute Module's bootloader, a neat way into how the Pi boots over USB.

brief.what_it_is: rpiboot is a host-side command-line tool, built from C source with make against libusb, that talks to a Raspberry Pi over USB while the device is in its ROM USB boot mode. It acts as a file server, sending boot firmware and a boot image into the device's memory. The default payload is a Linux-based mass-storage-gadget, which makes the Pi's storage appear to the host as a standard USB drive. An OS image can then be written to that drive with Raspberry Pi Imager. On Compute Module 4 and newer, it is also used to update the bootloader SPI flash EEPROM.
brief.why_it_exists: The README says rpiboot 'provides a file server for loading software into memory on a Raspberry Pi for provisioning.' The aim is to get at a Pi's storage or bootloader from a host computer over USB, without needing a working OS on the device.
brief.how_it_works: The host uses libusb to talk to the Pi, and the Pi's boot ROM is put into usbboot mode, either by a nRPIBOOT/EMMC-DISABLE jumper, a GPIO set up in OTP on Pi 4B and Pi 400, or by holding the power button on Pi 5, Pi 500 and Pi 500+. rpiboot then sends the chosen firmware or initramfs payload. The mass-storage-gadget boots a Linux initramfs that scans for SD/EMMC, NVMe and USB block devices and uses configfs to expose them as USB mass-storage devices. The legacy msd firmware instead exposes the SD/EMMC device as an emulated mass-storage device, with no console and slower writes.

commands_seen.context: Boots the device with the Linux-based mass-storage-gadget payload from the named directory; this is the recommended way to launch it on Pi 5, Pi 500 and Pi 500+ after the power-button step.
Boots the device with the legacy msd firmware instead of the Linux gadget; the README says this is for Pi 4 and older devices.
Run from the recovery directory on a Compute Module 4; the -j flag writes OTP metadata JSON into the metadata directory.
Clones the repository with its rpi-eeprom submodule, using a shallow clone.
Builds the rpiboot binary from the cloned usbboot directory on Linux.

macOS build command; the README recommends installing to /usr/local rather than /usr/bin on macOS.
Builds an SD card image that permanently sets GPIO 8 as nRPIBOOT on a Pi 4B or Pi 400. The README warns this change to OTP cannot be undone.
Installs kpartx, a Linux-only dependency needed for the Pi 4 GPIO SD-card utility.

brief.install_notes: Clone with --recurse-submodules because rpi-eeprom is a git submodule, and set the system date correctly so git does not fail. On Linux, install libusb-1.0 dev files and pkg-config as above, then run make. sudo is not needed if your user can write to /dev/bus/usb. On macOS, install libusb and pkg-config with Homebrew and set PKG_CONFIG_PATH if libusb.h is not found; on ARM Macs the README gives a fallback of building libusb 1.0.27 from source. Windows 11 uses Cygwin, the symlinks need core.symlinks set to true, and the rpiboot driver installer must be run once from win32\rpiboot_setup. Homebrew also packages it as 'rpiboot'; its caveat says to run sudo rpiboot -d "$(brew --prefix rpiboot)"/share/rpiboot/mass-storage-gadget64. Compute Modules need a jumper fitted (EMMC-DISABLE/nRPIBOOT) before power-on. Pi 500 needs its QMK keyboard firmware updated via raspi-config to get the power-button entry.
brief.standout: The Pi's own boot ROM is turned into a USB mass-storage device, and the default payload is a small Linux initramfs that exposes its SD, eMMC and NVMe storage through configfs and also gives a console over UART and USB CDC-UART. The same tool also updates bootloader EEPROM and can provision secure boot.
brief.status: unknown for exact dates: the fetched page showed no last-commit date and no release date. The README covers current hardware (Compute Module 5, Pi 500+, Raspberry Pi OS Trixie), and the repo has 516 commits, about 1.4k stars and 313 forks, which points to active upkeep, but I could not confirm recency.
brief.caveats: Primarily Linux. The README says it is widely used on Linux x86, Windows 11 via Cygwin, and macOS, but other platforms are 'best-effort and/or community-maintained'. The Pi 4B and Pi 400 GPIO setup permanently modifies OTP and cannot be changed afterwards. Legacy msd firmware has no console and slower writes. The Pi 4 GPIO utility depends on kpartx and so is Linux-only. The FreeBSD section shows 'mdo' where 'sudo' is probably meant. Power must be fully removed, not shut down, before the Pi 5 USB-C connection. Licence is Apache-2.0.
